Selling a Canadian home: map the principal-residence years and the reporting step

See how Canada’s one-plus-year formula translates designation years into a gain shield, why one family-unit year cannot normally be assigned to two homes, and why a fully exempt sale still has a reporting step.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 6 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

The central idea

The principal-residence exemption depends on qualifying and designating years, residence status and the ownership period. A gain that looks fully exempt still needs to be reported under current CRA rules.

01

The formula turns qualifying years into a fraction

CRA’s technical Income Tax Folio describes the principal-residence formula as A × (B ÷ C). A is the gain otherwise determined before this reduction; B is the number of eligible designated years, with a possible one-year addition; and C is the number of tax years ending after the acquisition date during which the taxpayer owned the property.

For dispositions under the current rule, B generally includes one extra year when the taxpayer was resident in Canada in the year containing the acquisition date, plus the qualifying years when the property was designated as the principal residence and the taxpayer was resident. The Folio says “during” the acquisition year means at any time in that year, not necessarily throughout the year. If the taxpayer was not resident during that year, the formula does not give the extra year. The exact result also depends on the legal definition of the acquisition date and residence; the model uses user-entered year counts to make the arithmetic visible.

Consider an original hypothetical: a CAD 300,000 gain, 20 ownership tax years after acquisition, 15 qualifying designated tax years counted before the addition, and Canadian residence in the acquisition year. B is 16, so the formula fraction is 16 ÷ 20, or 80%. The formula shields CAD 240,000; CAD 60,000 of gain remains before any capital-gains inclusion or income-tax calculation. It is not a tax bill.

02

A year must qualify, and a family unit generally has one home per year

A housing unit can qualify for a year when it is owned by the taxpayer and the taxpayer, their current or former spouse or common-law partner, or a child ordinarily lived in it at some time during that year; it must also be designated. A year count is not simply a count of months in a home.

For 1982 and later years, CRA says only one home may be designated as a family’s principal residence for each year. The family-unit rules can connect a taxpayer, spouse or common-law partner, and certain children. This matters when a household owns a house and a cottage, holds two homes during a move, or sells multiple homes. Assigning a year to one property can affect the designation available when another property is disposed of later.

The explorer models one property at a time. It does not optimize which property should receive a year, allocate jointly owned gains between owners, determine whether a home qualifies, or calculate a household’s family-unit status. Those decisions need the actual ownership and residence history across every relevant property.

03

The “plus one” rule helps in a move year, but does not designate two homes

CRA’s current worked example describes a Canadian resident who sells a principal residence and buys another home in the same calendar year. The plus-one rule can treat both properties as eligible for the principal-residence exemption for that year, even though only one property may be designated as the family’s principal residence for that year. The taxpayer should keep the designation decision because it can affect the later sale of the new home.

The acquisition-year residence condition matters: CRA says the purchaser must be resident in Canada during the year the new principal residence is purchased to use the extra year. Do not count a bonus year simply because two homes overlapped. A person who was non-resident throughout the acquisition year does not qualify for this addition under CRA’s explanation.

In the single-property model, “resident in Canada in the acquisition year?” switches the one-year addition on or off. It does not test immigration status, tax residence, whether a property qualifies, or the same-year purchase-and-sale facts. Use the question as a sensitivity, not as a legal conclusion.

04

An exempt gain still has to be reported

For dispositions from 2016 onward, CRA says it will only allow the principal-residence exemption when the disposition and designation are reported on the income-tax return. Its current page’s latest detailed form instructions cover a 2025 disposition: report the sale on Schedule 3 and complete Form T2091(IND). Where a property was the principal residence for all ownership years or all but one, CRA says only page 1 of T2091(IND) is required under that guide.

CRA says a late designation can be accepted in certain circumstances, but a penalty may apply. If the sale was omitted, its guidance says to ask CRA to amend the return for the disposition year. The requirement to report a disposition is separate from whether the formula leaves any gain to tax. A principal-residence loss is generally not deductible because the home is personal-use property.

Report a disposition in the calendar year it occurs. Because CRA’s linked form guide currently details the 2025 tax return, verify the form and line references for the year you file. Trusts use different forms; a legal representative of a deceased owner may need Form T1255.

05

Keep rental use, deemed sales and special histories out of a simple year-count model

A home used partly to earn income may require a reasonable split of proceeds and adjusted cost base between personal and income-producing portions. A change from personal to rental use, or the reverse, can create a deemed disposition at fair market value. Elections under subsections 45(2) or 45(3) may change timing when their conditions are met, but they have specific filing and capital-cost-allowance restrictions.

Other cases need separate analysis: a property acquired before 1972, a 1994 capital-gains election, non-residence, a trust, a death, more than one property sold in a year, and Canada’s residential flipping rule. CRA says a housing unit held for fewer than 365 consecutive days can generally fall under a rule that treats the gain as business income, subject to listed life-event exceptions. The principal-residence exemption does not turn that rule into a simple capital-gain fraction.

Use the four figures to understand the basic designated-year arithmetic. They are original hypothetical scenarios; the chart does not calculate taxable income, the inclusion rate, tax payable, provincial tax, ownership shares or eligibility. For an actual sale or deemed disposition, check CRA’s current guide and get tax advice for the complete property history.
